newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Peters' pension plan takes predictable blow.
newsitem.headline: NZ Peters' pension plan takes predictable blow.

text.p: Treasurer Winston Peters' proposed compulsory retirement savings scheme (CRSS) took its biggest blow on Thursday when a government-appointed review group reported, as expected, that the current taxpayer-funded scheme could be maintained with gradual changes.

Opposition politicians said interim report of the 1997 Periodic Report Group (PRG), coming after the scheme was rejected by the Consumers Institute and several prominent cabinet ministers, effectively undermined Peters' plan.

"It is not the final nail in the coffin of the plan -- that has already been driven in. It is the largest lump of earth descending on the coffin as it goes down," Labour's finance spokesman Michael Cullen said.
But Peters was unfazed, saying the report confirmed the current pay-as-you-go pension scheme was unsustainable.
"I welcome that report. I think it's wonderful," Peters said at a press conference after its release.
"It's crunch time now. Tell New Zealanders with precision what they will get and how they will get it," Peters challenged his critics.
But he refused to be drawn on what he would advocate if a referendum in September rejected the CRSS.
The government, a coalition between Peters' nationalist New Zealand First Party and the larger conservative National Party, is committed to implementing the referendum outcome.
It is seen as a key defining issue for Peters and his party, who have seen their support plummet since signing the coalition deal in December.
Opinion polls indicate the CRSS, which would require savings funded by broadly equivalent tax cuts to be invested in an annuity, will be overwhelmingly rejected.
The coalition agreed individual MPs would have the right to speak for or against the scheme ahead of the referendum.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger has thrown his support behind the CRSS, but that has drawn criticism from his own backbenchers, who overwhelmingly oppose compulsion, and raised questions about his future leadership.
Leadership aspirant Jenny Shipley, the State Services minister, has made a strong play of her opposition to the scheme.

In parliament on Thursday National backbencher John Banks asked Bolger: "Does the Prime Minister yet understand and accept that people who know something about these matters don't agree with him, and when will he give away his uninformed support for this fatally flawed proposal or is it a case of where Winston goes, I go?"
On Wednesday Environment Minister Simon Upton attacked the scheme, saying it was based on unrealistic assumptions.

"The belief that tax cuts equivalent to eight cents in the dollar can be delivered while the budget is kept in surplus and taxpayer top-ups are fully funded as lump sums...is in my view a pipe dream," Upton said.
On Thursday Social Welfare Minister Roger Sowry backed the PRG's findings, saying the current scheme with periodic reviews would provide as much security as any compulsory scheme.
The PRG report concluded New Zealand Superannuation (NZS) was sustainable with some gradual changes to meet the demands placed on the scheme by an ageing population after 2015.
"The tide is coming in but it is not an unexpected or unpredictable tsunami," said Jeff Todd, the Auckland accountant chairing PRG.
"Careful preparation is needed but we don't need to dismantle what we have in place."

The PRG said NZS currently cost about four percent of Gross Domestic Product net of tax each year and would start to rise once baby boomers retired in increasing numbers around 2015. That cost would reach about nine percent of GDP in 2050.
"We don't think this will create an economic crisis though. Many other OECD countries are facing even stronger pressures on their public pension schemes," the PRG said.

Options for ensuring NZS stayed affordable included reducing debt levels now, raising the age of eligibility, and paying less publicly-provided superannuation to those who could provide for themselves in retirement.
Another option was continuing to index NZS to cover inflation, but not linking it fully to average earnings, which tended to grow faster.
